n: After the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew turns from Jesus’s words to his works. Chapters 8–9 gather a series of miracles showing his power over disease, nature, evil, and death.
A leper kneels before Jesus. He doesn’t doubt Jesus’s power — only whether Jesus is willing to help someone like him.

f.g: Leprosy in the Bible covered various skin diseases; sufferers were ritually unclean and lived apart from society.
if thou wilt = if you are willing.

n: Jesus touches the untouchable. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean, but here Jesus’s touch makes the leper clean instead.
Jesus sends the man to the priest to follow the law of Moses for cleansed lepers. Being officially declared clean would restore him to his family and community.

f.g: Jesus often discouraged publicity, perhaps to avoid crowds seeking only signs or stirring political hopes.

n: In Capernaum, Jesus’s home base in Galilee, a Roman army officer comes to him for help — a Gentile reaching out to a Jewish teacher.

f.g: A Roman officer commanding about 100 soldiers.

n: The centurion’s servant is paralyzed and suffering badly. That a powerful officer cares so much for a servant says something about his character.

f.g: palsy = paralysis.

n: Jesus immediately offers to go to the Gentile’s house — something many Jews would have avoided to stay ritually clean.

f.w: I will come and heal him

n: The centurion humbly says he isn’t worthy to host Jesus. He believes Jesus’s word alone is enough to heal, even from a distance.
As a soldier he understands authority: orders given are orders carried out. He recognizes that Jesus has that kind of authority over sickness.

f.w: I am a man under authority
f.g: He serves under higher command and also commands others — so he knows how authority works.

n: Jesus is amazed. This outsider shows more faith than he has found among his own covenant people.
Jesus foresees people from every nation joining the patriarchs at God’s great feast. Faith, not ancestry, opens the kingdom.

f.g: Literally “recline,” as guests did at a banquet table.

n: Those who assumed they belonged by birth may be shut out if they reject him. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” describes the bitter regret of the lost.

f.g: Those who by lineage were heirs to the covenant — here, Israelites who reject the Messiah.
Grinding the teeth in anguish or anger.

n: Jesus grants the request exactly as the centurion believed, and the servant is healed at that very moment, without Jesus ever entering the house.

f.g: selfsame = the very same.

n: At Peter’s home in Capernaum, Jesus finds Peter’s mother-in-law in bed with a fever. This quiet detail also shows Peter was married.
A simple touch heals her completely — no lingering weakness — and she rises at once to serve. Healing leads naturally to service.

f.g: ministered = served, likely by preparing food and caring for guests.

n: As evening falls, crowds bring the sick and the possessed. Jesus heals them all by his word.

f.g: even = evening. Mark notes it was the sabbath, which ended at sunset.

n: Matthew sees these healings as fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy about the suffering Servant who would carry our burdens — physical as well as spiritual.

f.g: Esaias = Isaiah (Greek form of the name).

n: Seeing the crowds, Jesus decides to cross the Sea of Galilee to the eastern shore.

f.g: The eastern, largely Gentile shore of the Sea of Galilee.

n: A scribe eagerly promises to follow Jesus anywhere. Jesus will test whether he has counted the cost.

f.g: An expert in the law of Moses; most scribes opposed Jesus, making this offer unusual.
whithersoever = wherever.

n: Jesus warns that following him means giving up comfort and security. Even animals have homes, but he has none.

f.g: Jesus’s favorite title for himself, echoing Daniel 7:13; in LDS teaching it also points to him as Son of the Man of Holiness, God the Father.

n: Another disciple asks to wait until he has buried his father — possibly meaning until his father dies, which could be years away.

f.g: suffer = allow, permit.

n: Jesus’s startling reply puts discipleship first: let the spiritually dead take care of such matters; the call to follow can’t wait.

f.w: let the dead bury their dead
f.g: Likely meaning: let those who are spiritually dead bury the physically dead.

n: Jesus gets into a boat, and his disciples follow — they are literally “following” him into what will become a test of faith.

f.g: A fishing boat; one from this era was found in the Sea of Galilee in 1986, about 27 feet long.

n: A sudden violent storm swamps the boat, yet Jesus sleeps. The Sea of Galilee lies low among hills, and fierce winds can drop onto it without warning.

f.g: Greek seismos — literally a “shaking,” the word often used for earthquakes.

n: Terrified, the disciples wake him with a short, desperate prayer: “Lord, save us: we perish.”
Jesus first calms the disciples’ fear, then the sea. With a word he rebukes wind and waves, and everything goes still.

f.w: rebuked the winds and the sea

n: The disciples ask the right question. In the Old Testament only God rules the sea — so who is this man?

f.w: What manner of man is this

n: On the eastern shore two violently possessed men live among the tombs, terrorizing the area. Mark and Luke focus on one of them.

f.g: Other manuscripts read Gadarenes or Gerasenes — towns in the region east of the sea.
Tombs were unclean places; living there marked these men as outcasts.

n: The evil spirits recognize Jesus as the Son of God before most people do, and they fear the judgment they know is coming.

f.g: Before the appointed day of final judgment.

f.w: What have we to do with thee
f.g: An idiom meaning “Why are you bothering us?”

n: A large herd of pigs is feeding nearby — a sign this was a Gentile area, since Jews didn’t raise unclean animals.
The spirits beg to enter the pigs. Latter-day Saint teaching notes that spirits without bodies crave one — even an animal’s.

f.g: besought = begged.

n: With one word, “Go,” Jesus frees the men. The herd stampedes into the sea — showing how destructive these spirits were.

f.g: A steep slope or cliff above the lake.

n: The herdsmen run to town and report everything, both the lost pigs and the healed men.

f.g: The herdsmen.

n: Rather than rejoice, the townspeople ask Jesus to leave. Perhaps their financial loss or fear of his power mattered more to them than two restored lives.

f.g: coasts = borders, region (not seashore).
